Common pediatric surgical problems

Objectives:

-Introduction. -Abdominal wall defects.

-Embryology. * Umblical Hernia

-Inguinal hernia. *Omphalocele (Exomphalos)

-Hydrocele. *Gastroschisis.

-Undescended testis.

-Circumcision.

Introduction:

-Inguinal hernia, hydrocele and undescended tesis are common groin condition in infants and children.

-They share a common embryological orgin.

-They may present in isolation or combination in the same patient.

-Accurate clinical distinction is very important as the management and outcome is different in each condition.

What is process vaginalis (PV) ?

Is outpoutching of peritoneum at deep ring and extends through inguinal canal down to scrotum, associated with normal descend of testis. At 36-40 of gestation the testis reaches the scrotum and PV gradually obliterates.

Embryology:

Inguinal Hernia

Definition:

is an indirect hernia related to failure of closure of the patent processus vaginalis (PPV) at the deep inguinal ring. Intra-abdominal contents pass within a PPV, through the deep inguinal ring, inguinal canal, superficial inguinal ring and potentially into the scrotum (male) or via the canal of Nuck to the labium (female)

  • Incidence:
  • -Approximately 1-5% of all children will develop IH.
  • Newborns incidence 3-5%.
  • Over all incidence in premature infants 10-30%.
  • Positive family history in about 10%.
  • More common in boys than girls ( 5 :1).
  • In boys, rt sided found in 60% ,lt sided in 30% and bilateral in 10%.
  • In girls , laterality is equal.

Inguinal Hernia:

  • Risk Factors:
  • -prematurity.
  • -connective tissue disorders.
  • ventriculo-peritoneal shunt (VP shunt).
  • -peritoneal dialysis(PD).
  • Ascites ( any conditions cause increase intra-abdominal pressure).
  • Undescended testis.
  • -others

Inguinal Hernia

  • Clinical presentation:
  • Most hernias are asymptomatic except for intermittent inguinal bulging with straining ( crying, coughing ,defecation ,etc. )
  • They are often found by parents .
  • Inguinal Pain is rare unless hernia gets complicated.
  • On examination, often the hernia is reduced and no bulge is seen. Provocative manoeuver such as standing , coughing, laughing or jumping are required to elicit it.
  • Examination should include scrotum and testes.

-

-

-

-

  • History of a bulge on crying but nothing on examination, testes descended → refer to the paediatric surgery clinic (a convincing history is enough; it won't resolve). 435 ×2
  • Clinical presentation:(Incareceration/Irreducability)
  • The inciedence range from 12-17 %.
  • Younger age(below 6 months) and prematurity are risk factors.
  • As fussy infant with intermittent abdominal pain and vomiting.
  • A tender and sometime erythermatous irreducible mass is noted in the groin.
  • Incarceration may be the first presenting sign of the hernia.
  • On examination , the infant is usually irritable, in pain, with tender groin swelling which can not be reduced with gentle pressure.
  • Incarceration will result in bowel obstruction and if not treated will progress to strangulation( bowel ischemia).
  • Severe pain , prolonged incarceration,fever, tachycardia, and vomiting are suggestive of strangulation (rare presentation)
  • Known hernia, irreducible for 6 hours, no skin changes → incarcerated inguinal hernia (not strangulated). 439 ×3
  • Management:(Uncomplicated IH)
  • IH will not resolve spontaneously and surgery is only the treatment .
  • Open inguinal herniotomy ( more common approach) .
  • Laparoscopic herniotomy ( less popular) .
  • Preterm babies usually have their hernias repaired before discharge from nursery to avoid incarceration.
  • Infants and children should have their surgery done within weeks ( OR availability ) .
  • 2-month-old with a reducible inguinal hernia → herniotomy as early as possible. 439 ×7
  • Management:(Incarcerated IH)
  • The presence of peritonitis or septic shock is an absolute contraindication to attempted reduction.
  • Intravenous access and rehydration.
  • Monitored conscious sedation.
  • Firm and continuous pressure is applied around the incarceration.
  • Successful reduction is usually confirmed by sudden pop of contents back to abdominal cavity.
  • Over 90-95% of incarcerated IH can be successfully reduced.
  • Once hernia is reduced ,a delay of 24-48h is allowed before herniotomy (resolution of edema and inflammation)
  • Urgent operation ( Herniotomy ) is necessary if reduction fails.

Technique for reduction

  • Frog-leg position
  • Push down towards pubis w/ left fingers
  • push up towards canal w/ right fingers
  • maintain gentle pressure along the inguinal canal
  • 1-year-old, right testis in the inguinal canal → orchidopexy (he is already past 6 months). 441 ×4

CONGENITAL HYDROCELE

  • Definition:
  • An abnormal collection of fluid in the process virginals which fails to obliterate resulting in swelling in the scrotum and groin.
  • Approximately 5% of boys at term have hydrocele.
  • Less common in girls and known as a hydrocele of the canal of nuck.

Types of Hydrocele

CONGENITAL HYDROCELE

  • Clinical presentation:
  • Painless scrotal or groin swelling , but mostly scrotal.
  • Increase in size following viral infection.
  • On examination , tense , overlying skin is often has a blue tinge. Not reducable , transilluminte , difficult to palpate the testis separately.
  • What separates an elective hernia from an emergency → reducibility. 435
Added explanationVaricocele = dilated pampiniform venous plexus, usually left-sided in adolescents: "bag of worms", dragging ache worse on standing/activity, disappears lying down, does not transilluminate, and you can get above it.
Added explanationIn an adult, a new tense scrotal swelling must have a scrotal ultrasound first — a secondary hydrocele can hide a testicular tumour (or epididymo-orchitis) — before any aspiration or repair.

Various Hydroceles

  • Management:
  • Expectant management(observation) in the first two years of age.
  • By the age of 2 years 90% of hydoceles will have resolved.
  • Surgery ( hydrocelectomy /high ligation of PPV) is indicated if the hydrocele fails to resolve by age of 2 years.

UNDESCENDED TESTIS (CRYPTORCHDISM)

Embryology:

  • Normal testis developed from gonadonephric ridge .
  • Normal testis descends across the abdomen to deep inguinal ring between 8-15 weeks of gestation under control of AMH.
  • Second phase of descent , the testis moves through the inguinal canal into the scrotum (25-35 weeks of gestation) under control of androgens.
  • Testicular development and descent depend on interaction among endocrine, paracrine, growth and mechanical factors.

Embryology:

  • Definition:
  • Undescended testis (UDT): is arrested along its normal path of descent.
  • Retractile testis: is a testicle that may move back and forth between the scrotum and the groin .can be manipulated into scrotum where it remains without tension.
  • Ectopic testis: is located outside of normal path of descent.
Added explanationRetractile testis = a normal testis pulled up by an active cremasteric reflex: it can be brought down into the scrotum and stays there briefly before rising again — no surgery, just follow-up. A true UDT cannot be brought down to the scrotum. An ectopic testis lies off the line of descent (perineum, thigh, pubic area).
  • 6-year-old, testis "sometimes not in the scrotum", easily brought down but moves back up → retractile testis. 441 ×4
  • UDT felt as a mass in the groin — pre-op imaging → no further radiological imaging is needed. 439 ×2

Incidence:

-UDT occurs in approximately 1-3% of term infants and 33-45% of premature infants.

  • Occurs on the rt side in 50% , lt side 35%, bilateral 10-15%.
  • Regarding UDT, the true statement → orchiopexy is best done at 6–12 months. 427

Clinical presentation:

  • Empty scrotum.
  • -Absence of one or both testes.
  • Swelling in the groin ( testis or hernia).
  • On examination, hemi-scrotum is underdeveloped/ hypo plastic
  • Testis is palpable in the groin and fails to comedown to scrotum in 80% of cases.
  • Testis is impalpable /non- palpable in the remaining 20% of cases ( intra-abdominal , atrophied , or agenesis).

Management:

UNDESCENDED TESTIS (CRYPTORCHDISM)

A- Hormonal treatment:

The role of hormonal therapy is controversial.

LHRH and HCG are used with varying degree of success.

B- Surgical treatment ( orchidopexy ) the treatment of choice.

The best timing is between 6-12 months of age.

UNDESCENDED TESTIS (CRYPTORCHDISM

Management :

  • B- Surgical treatment :
    • Palpable unilateral or bilateral → orchidopexy.
    • Impalpable/ nonpalpable :
    • Radiographic imaging (US , CT, MRI)

is rarely helpful in locating nonpalpable testis .

  • Diagnostic laparoscopy is the preferred approach
    • If testis is intra-abdominal Lap assisted orchidopexy .
    • If atrophic inguinal exploration and excision.
    • if agenesis nothing to be done

– Palpable unilateral or bilateral → orchidopexy.

– Impalpable/ nonpalpable :

  • 3-month-old, testis palpable in the inguinal region → best time for orchidopexy between 6 and 12 months. 436 ×6
  • 6-month-old, left testis not palpable → best modality to localize it → diagnostic laparoscopy. 435 ×6

UNDESCENDED TESTIS (CRYPTORCHDISM)

  • Indication for surgery : (benefit of orchidopexy )
  • To optimize fertility.
  • To potentially reduce malignancy rate (controversial)
  • To place testis in examinable position to detect malignancy early.
  • To reduce risk of torsion.
  • To reduce risk of trauma.
  • To optimize hormonal function.
  • To repair the associated hernia( 90% of UDT )
  • For cosmetic and psychological reasons.

ACUTE SCROTUM

Definition:

Acute scrotal pain with or without swelling and erythema.

  • 15-year-old, left scrotal swelling with dragging pain on activity, disappears supine, transillumination negative, can get above it → varicocele. 437 ×4
  • 24-year-old, painful scrotal swelling for 1 month, tense swollen right testicle → first step ultrasonography. 437 ×2

Anatomy

Anatomy of the normal (right) testis and spermatic cord.

  • Groin swelling by history, none on exam, but thickened right spermatic cord with a cough impulse → no imaging required — the diagnosis is clinical. 436

DDx of an acute scrotum

ACUTE SCROTUM

  • Torsion of the testis.
    • Torsion of the appendix testis /epididymis.
    • Epididymitis / orchitis.
    • Idiopathic scrotal edema ( dermatitis, insect bite )
    • Inguinal hernia (incarcerated).
    • Trauma /sexual abuse.
    • Vasculitis ( Henoch-schonlein purpura).
    • Cellulitis.
    • Others.

– Torsion of the testis.

– Torsion of the appendix testis /epididymis.

– Epididymitis / orchitis.

– Inguinal hernia (incarcerated).

– Trauma /sexual abuse.

– Vasculitis ( Henoch-schonlein purpura).

– Cellulitis.

– Others.

ACUTE SCROTUM

Approach to acute scrotum:

  • Early recognition and prompt managent are very important because of the possibility of testicular torsion as the etiology with permanent damage to the testis.
  • 1- History :
  • Timing (time of onset and length)
  • Pain character, onset and course (sudden vs gradual, constant vs intermittent)
  • Location (testes, scrotum or abdomen)
  • Quality (sharp, dull)
  • History of trauma.

Approach to acute scrotum:

2- Examination:

  • Overall inspection of patient and comfort level
  • Abdominal, inguinal, and genital exam required
  • Test the cremasteric reflex first

Absence of reflex may be most sensitive indicator of torsion of the testes

  • Begin with unaffected side
  • Palpate testes, spermatic cord, epididymis and inguinal region.
  • Evaluate lie, size, masses and mobility of testis.

Approach to acute scrotum:

2- Investigations:

NORMAL

TORSION

  • Done when testicular torsion is difficult to diagnosis.
    • Urine analysis.
    • Us with color flow Doppler. (sensitivity 90% specificity 99%).
    • radionuclular imaging ( Sensitivity 90-100%)

Imagimg studies should not delay scrotal exploration

when there is a high suspicion of torsion.

MANAGEMENT:

ACUTE SCROTUM

Testicular torsion:(the only surgical cause)

  • Testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis.
  • Imaging studies usually are not necessary and ordering them may waste valuable time when the definitive treatment is surgical.
  • Timing is critical 4-6 H.
  • Scrotal exploration if any doubt.
  • If testis is viable untwist anticlockwise and fix both sides.
  • If testis is is not viable needs excision and fix the other side.

Fixing contralateral testis to reduce the torsion in the future.

Golden period < 6 hours since onset of pain

MANAGEMENT:

ACUTE SCROTUM

Other causes:( non-surgical)

  • Epididymoorchitis : Antibiotics.
  • Torsion of appendix testis/epididymis :self limiting condition , if discover before exploration can be treated conservatively ,but if found at exploration needs excision.

ACUTE SCROTUM

Other causes:( non-surgical)

  • Idiopathic scrotal edema: Self limiting condition treated with analgesia and observation.
  • Traumatic orchitis : conservative treatment.

Go By

Protocol for the diagnosis and treatment of the acute scrotum.

History, physical examination and urinalysis

Short duration of symptoms and negative urinalysis: high probability of torsionLong duration of symptoms and positive urinalysis: low probability of torsion
↓ Surgical exploration↓ Color Doppler ultrasonography
→ Decreased or absent blood flow or equivocal results ↓ Surgical exploration
→ Increased or normal blood flow ↓ Nonoperative management or observation

Abdominal Wall Defects.

Umbilical Hernia:

  • Mostly present at birth ( congenital ).
  • Due to failure of umbilical ring closure.

-Incidence ranges 2-18%. More common in black.

-common in hypothyroidism, and some syndromes like down syndrome, beckwith-wiedman and others.

-Most umbilical hernia will close spontaneously (50-95%).

-Very safe to observe the hernia until age of 4-6 yrs.

-Surgical repair is indicated in cases failed to close or developed complications.

  • 5-year-old, umbilical swelling since birth, reducible, 1-cm defect → surgical repair. 439 ×3

What is circumcision?

  • Removal of redundant foreskin (prepuce)

Indications of circumcision

  • Religious or cultural
  • Pathologic phimosis: inability to retract the foreskin
  • Paraphimosis: inability to reduce retracted foreskin
  • Balantitis xerotica obliterans
  • Recurrent balanitis
  • Recurrent posthitis

Contraindications to circumcision

  • Very short penis
  • Hypospadias
  • Epispadias
  • Chordee
  • Burried penis

Techniques

  • Plastibell (newborn)
  • Gomco clamp
  • Mogen clamp
  • Sleeve technique
Added explanationMethods: device techniques (e.g. Plastibell, Gomco clamp) in infants, or a freehand (dorsal-slit / sleeve) excision — older children usually under general anaesthesia.

Complication

  • Bleeding
    • Infection
    • Penile adhesions
    • Inclusion cysts
    • Urethral fistula
    • Amputation
    • Penile necrosis (Never use monopolar electrocautery!!)

Common pediatric surgical problems

  • Inguinal hernia.

Inguinal hernia

Notes

1. Inguinal Hernia

Definition

A hernia is the protrusion/outpouching of an organ or tissue outside its containing wall. Any groin or scrotal swelling should prompt inguinal hernia as a major differential.

Notes

Direct vs. Indirect Hernia

TYPEPATHWAYTYPICAL POPULATION
IndirectEnters internal ring → travels through inguinal canal → exits external ringAdults and children — predominant type in pediatrics
DirectProtrudes directly through the abdominal wall / inguinal triangleAdults only
Notes

Adult vs. Pediatric Hernia — Different Diseases

FEATUREADULT HERNIAPEDIATRIC HERNIA
CauseAcquired — abdominal wall weakness ± ↑ intra-abdominal pressureCongenital — patent processus vaginalis (PPV)
Why not muscular?—Child is too young to have developed wall weakness
  • 6-month-old, bilateral scrotal swellings, can get above them, transillumination positive — cause → patent processus vaginalis. 438
Notes

Processus Vaginalis & Mechanism

The testis descends from the abdomen → internal ring → inguinal canal → external ring → scrotum, accompanied by the processus vaginalis, which should normally close around/before birth. Persistent patency creates a tract between abdomen and scrotum → indirect inguinal hernia. Contents may include bowel, fat, or gonadal structures.

  • Boy with a groin lump extending into the scrotum, positive internal ring occlusion test → indirect inguinal hernia. 436
Notes

Presentation

CLASSIC PICTURE
Painless, intermittent inguinal/scrotal swelling that enlarges with ↑ intra-abdominal pressure or straining, and may reduce spontaneously when the child relaxes.
Notes

Natural History

KEY TEACHING POINT
Inguinal hernia has no spontaneous resolution — the PPV remains patent. Swelling may temporarily disappear, but the underlying hernia persists and carries a significant complication risk, so it always requires surgical repair.
Notes

Complications of Inguinal Hernia

Incarceration — hernia cannot be reduced back into the abdomen (incarceration ≈ irreducibility)
Obstruction — herniated bowel becomes obstructed
Strangulation — compromised blood supply → ischemia; represents progression of an incarcerated hernia with vascular compromise

Presentation of Incarceration / Obstruction (Emergency)

Pain / excessive crying in infants
Vomiting
Abdominal distension
Failure to pass stool
Local swelling
Redness + marked tenderness over the hernia
EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT
NPO, IV fluids, good analgesia, then attempt manual reduction.
If it reduces: converts from emergency → elective, but do NOT discharge — keep the child admitted and book surgery for the next available slot.
If it does not reduce: immediate surgery — risk of bowel ischemia.
  • 3-month-old booked for herniotomy, now irritable, poor feeding, persistent swelling for 3 h → trial of hernia reduction under sedation and analgesia. 435 ×8 432 ×6
Notes

Timing of Repair

Uncomplicated pediatric inguinal hernia → elective surgery as soon as reasonably available. Not an immediate emergency, but should not be left for prolonged observation because it will not resolve spontaneously and complications can occur.

SAFETY-NETTING
If surgery must be delayed for scheduling reasons, explicitly counsel parents on obstruction/incarceration symptoms and to seek urgent care if these develop.

Hydrocele

Types of Hydrocele

Notes

2. Hydrocele

Mechanism

A hydrocele is fluid accumulation around the testis. In infants this reflects a small patent processus vaginalis — the opening is too small for bowel to pass, so only fluid does — combined with immature lymphatic/fluid absorption, creating a relative imbalance between fluid production and absorption. Absorption improves as the lymphatic system matures.

Notes

Communicating vs. Non-communicating

TYPEMECHANISM
CommunicatingSmall PPV remains connected to the abdominal cavity — fluid communicates with the scrotum
Non-communicatingFluid confined around the testis, no ongoing abdominal communication
PPV SIZE RULE OF THUMB
Larger PPV → bowel/tissue can enter → inguinal hernia. Smaller PPV → fluid only → hydrocele.
  • 6-month-old with bilateral non-communicating hydroceles → hydrocelectomy at 1–2 years if not resolved. 438 ×3
Notes

Natural History & Management

RESOLVES SPONTANEOUSLY
Most infant hydroceles improve as fluid absorption matures — many resolve within 6–12 months, or by up to 2 years if later. Uncomplicated hydrocele carries essentially no major complication risk → manage with observation, not early surgery. Persistent hydrocele beyond this window → operative treatment.
Notes

Hydrocele vs. Inguinal Hernia — High-Yield Exam Distinction

This distinction is very commonly examined in OSCEs and MCQs.

TESTHYDROCELEINGUINAL HERNIA
TransilluminationUsually transilluminates (fluid-filled)Generally does not
“Get above the swelling”Can get above it — confined to scrotumCannot get above it — continues toward inguinal canal
ReducibilityNot reducible (fluid collection)May be reducible
PITFALL
Transillumination can be misleading — e.g. a 4-year-old with scrotal trauma and a hematoma will not transilluminate (looks dark), which can be falsely read as "not a hydrocele." Transillumination should never be the sole discriminator.
MOST IMPORTANT CLINICAL SIGN
The “Can you get above the swelling?” sign is the most reliable bedside discriminator and a favorite exam question. Examine the groin– scrotum junction and attempt to palpate above the swelling from above/below:
Can get above it → swelling confined to scrotum → supports hydrocele
Cannot get above it → swelling continues into the inguinal canal → supports inguinal hernia

Hernial Sac

Notes

3. Pediatric Hernia Operation

FEATUREADULTSCHILDREN
ProcedureReduction + mesh repair (hernioplasty)Herniotomy — division/ligation of the processus vaginalis / hernial sac
WhyReinforces a weakened abdominal wallNo wall weakness to reinforce — the defect is the congenital patent PPV
Mesh needed?YesNo
  • Defect that causes an indirect inguinal hernia in children → patent processus vaginalis. 439
  • Father had mesh repair and wants mesh for his 3-month-old → mesh isn't required — the child needs herniotomy only. 438

Unilateral UDT

Notes

4. Undescended Testis (Cryptorchidism)

Examination Inspection

The affected hemiscrotum may appear smaller/poorly developed — described as a hypoplastic hemiscrotum (e.g. "hypoplastic left hemiscrotum"). Inspection alone cannot confirm undescended testis.

Palpation

Palpation is required to determine whether the testis is present and its location along the normal descent pathway: abdomen → inguinal canal/groin → near scrotum. If not palpable externally, consider an intra-abdominal location or an absent/atrophic testis.

  • 1-year-old, left testis in the inguinal region and can't be pulled down → undescended testis. 438

Intra-abdominal Testis

Notes

Timing

CURRENT APPROACH
Observe until about 6 months (spontaneous descent can still occur). Historical practice waited 1.5–2 years, but studies showed that if the testis has not descended by ~6–7 months, further spontaneous descent is unlikely. If still undescended → correct at approximately 6–9 months rather than prolonged waiting.
Doctor: correct at ~6–9 months. Exam options and guidelines (AUA/EAU): orchidopexy between 6 and 12 months (within 18 months at the latest). Same message — when 6–9 months isn't offered, choose 6–12 months; never "wait until puberty".
Notes

Complications if Left Untreated

Infertility / impaired testicular function
Testicular torsion — increased risk
Malignancy risk
Trauma — especially when superficial in the groin, more exposed to injury
Notes

Palpable vs. Non-palpable Testis

FINDINGIMPLICATION / NEXT STEP
Palpable (in groin)Location established clinically
Non- palpablePossibilities: intra-abdominal testis, absent/atrophic testis, or loss after intrauterine torsion. Ultrasound may show nonspecific structures and cannot reliably confirm a true testis.
KEY RULE
Diagnostic laparoscopy is the key investigation for a truly non-palpable testis — it is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

Abdominal wall defects

Notes

5. Umbilical Hernia

Pathogenesis

FEATUREADULTPEDIATRIC
CauseAcquired abdominal-wall weakness / ↑ intra-abdominal pressureFailure/delay of normal umbilical ring closure after cord clamping (congenital)
The umbilical cord is clamped after birth and the area normally closes by scar/fibrous tissue. Natural History & Management
RESOLVES SPONTANEOUSLY
Yes — the umbilical ring closes gradually as scar tissue matures. Incarceration and strangulation are extremely uncommon in children, so uncomplicated cases can safely be observed until approximately 4–5 years / preschool age (timing is flexible, not a fixed number). Persistent hernia at preschool age → consider operative closure.
Notes

Quick Timing Comparison

CONDITIONSPONTANEOUS RESOLUTION?MANAGEMENT TIMING
Inguinal herniaNeverElective repair soon after diagnosis
HydroceleUsually, yesObserve; most resolve by 6–12 months, up to 1–2 years if uncomplicated
Undescended testisOnly if earlyObserve to 6 months; correct at ~6–9 months if persistent
Umbilical herniaUsually, yesObserve until ~4–5 years / preschool age
  • 2-month-old with bilateral hernias and hydrocele → bilateral hernia repair and evacuation of the hydrocele. 434
  • 5-month-old with a reducible umbilical swelling → surgical repair between 4–5 years if not spontaneously resolved. 438 ×4
OmphaloceleGastroschisis
Notes

6. Congenital Abdominal Wall Defects

Noted by the professor as general awareness rather than a primary exam focus.

DEFECTDESCRIPTIONURGENCY
OmphaloceleCongenital abdominal wall defect centered at the umbilical region—
GastroschisisBowel protrudes through the abdominal wall, directly exposed to the atmosphereEmergency — exposed bowel vulnerable to contamination/bacteria
DANGER POINT
Gastroschisis is more urgent than omphalocele because the exposed bowel has no protective covering — it requires prompt management as an emergency.
Added explanationGastroschisis — defect usually right of the umbilical cord, no sac, usually isolated (bowel atresia the main association), young mothers. Omphalocele — central, covered by a sac with the cord inserting into it, may contain liver, and is often associated with other anomalies (cardiac, chromosomal, Beckwith–Wiedemann). At birth for gastroschisis: cover the bowel in a sterile bowel bag/cling film, keep warm, NG tube, IV fluids, urgent surgery.

7. Circumcision

A very common procedure, performed by urologists, pediatric surgeons, and other appropriately trained physicians.

Notes

Indications

Religious / cultural reasons — most common indication
Pathological phimosis — foreskin cannot be retracted due to scarring
Recurrent balanitis / balanoposthitis
Recurrent UTI, especially with urinary tract abnormalities
Recurrent paraphimosis
HIGH-YIELD CONTRAINDICATIONS
1. Hypospadias — the foreskin may be needed later for surgical repair 2. Bleeding disorder
  • 3-month-old with hypospadias brought for circumcision → don't circumcise — re-evaluate after 6 months (keep the foreskin for the hypospadias repair). 437 ×3
Notes

Complications

Bleeding — most common early complication
Infection
Pain / swelling
Meatal / urethral injury
Adhesions / skin bridges

Notes

Mastery Checklist

1 Pediatric inguinal hernia is congenital (patent processus vaginalis) and never resolves spontaneously — always needs surgical repair
(herniotomy, no mesh).
2 If an incarcerated hernia reduces manually, admit and book elective surgery — do not discharge; if it fails to reduce, operate immediately
(bowel ischemia risk).
3 Hydrocele in infants usually resolves spontaneously by 6–12 months (up to 2 years) — manage with observation, not surgery.
4 The "Can you get above the swelling?" sign is more reliable than transillumination for distinguishing hydrocele from hernia —
transillumination can be falsely negative (e.g. hematoma).
5 Larger PPV → hernia (bowel/tissue can enter); smaller PPV → hydrocele (fluid only).
6 Undescended testis: observe to 6 months, correct at 6–9 months if still undescended — risk of infertility, torsion, malignancy, and trauma if
untreated.
7 A truly non-palpable testis needs diagnostic laparoscopy (diagnostic + therapeutic) — ultrasound is not reliable.
8 Umbilical hernia is congenital (failed ring closure), almost never complicates, and is observed until 4–5 years.
9 Gastroschisis (exposed bowel, no sac) is a surgical emergency; omphalocele is covered and less urgent.
10 Never circumcise with hypospadias (foreskin needed for repair) or an active bleeding disorder.

Added explanationThyroglossal duct cyst — midline neck mass in a child that moves with swallowing and with tongue protrusion (attached to the hyoid by the tract). Treatment = Sistrunk operation: cyst + tract + central part of the hyoid, which keeps recurrence low.
  • 12-year-old, neck mass moving with swallowing and tongue protrusion → Sistrunk operation. 437 ×3
Added explanationCystic hygroma (macrocystic lymphatic malformation) — soft, compressible, brilliantly transilluminating swelling present at birth, classically in the posterior triangle of the neck. A branchial cyst is different: anterior border of sternocleidomastoid at the junction of its upper and middle thirds, usually seen in young adults, does not transilluminate brightly.
  • Neck swelling at birth, posterior triangle, transilluminates → cystic hygroma. 426
Added explanationJuvenile polyp — the commonest cause of painless rectal bleeding in toddlers (peak 2–5 years): streaks of bright blood on the stool with a normal anal examination; may prolapse. An anal fissure is the commonest cause in infants but is seen on examination (posterior midline tear) with pain on defecation.
  • 1-year-old, streaks of blood with stool for 2 weeks, normal examination → juvenile polyp. 438
Added explanationPerianal abscess in infants — almost always boys under 1 year; tender red perianal swelling → incision and drainage. Antibiotics alone don't treat an abscess; a fistula-in-ano may follow.
  • 6-month-old, 8-mm tender red perianal swelling for 2 days → incision and drainage with antibiotics for 5–7 days. 434 ×2
Added explanationInfantile haemangioma — absent or faint at birth, appears in the first weeks, grows rapidly (proliferative phase, first year), then slowly involutes. A port-wine stain (capillary malformation) is present at birth, flat, and grows with the child; an AV malformation is a fast-flow lesion, usually present at birth and enlarging later.
  • Small raised red lesion on the nose appearing slowly after birth → infantile haemangioma. 438
